stem:
The diagram shows square $S$ of side $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ and square $T$ of side $6\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Which claim correctly states how the area changes from $S$ to $T$?

options.text: The area of $T$ is twice the area of $S$ because the side length doubled.
The area of $T$ is four times the area of $S$ because the side length doubled.
The area of $T$ equals the area of $S$ because both shapes are squares.
The area of $T$ is six times the area of $S$, matching the new side length.

teacher.key_rationale: Area scales with the square of the side. Doubling the side multiplies area by 4: 9 cm² to 36 cm². Treating area as proportional to side, equal for all squares, or matching the new side length each miss that square factor.
teacher.figure_note: Added squares S (side 3) and T (side 6) side by side.
